Gaps flagged for next wave

Whether pain-neuroscience education delivers real-world benefit at scale and over years (shared with Section 14); the durability of graded-exposure / CBT / ACT gains beyond trial settings; acute:chronic workload as a prescriptive (not just descriptive) injury-prevention tool — the construct has been methodologically criticised and may not survive as a precise rule; whether any passive recovery modality (foam-rolling, massage guns, cupping, dry needling) beats placebo on a function endpoint vs. an acute-feel one; optimal loading dose/progression parameters for the major tendinopathies (no protocol is clearly superior yet); biomarkers or clinical signs that reliably identify who with sciatica/disc herniation actually benefits from early surgery; and the still-unsettled best management of nociplastic (centrally-driven) pain states beyond the multimodal stack.

Part V

27 — Surface & Sensory Specialties (Skin · Teeth & Mouth · Ear/Nose/Throat · Eye)

Manual section, v1.0 — 2026-06-28. Companion graded claims in 02-domains/surface-sensory-claims.json. This is the clinical-conditions companion to Section 11 (11-body-systems.md), which covered the longevity-lever view of skin (photoaging), mouth (periodontal–systemic), eye (AMD/cataract/glaucoma as dementia tails), and ear (ACHIEVE). Section 11 owns the anti-aging/prevention framing; this section owns the named diseases — acne, eczema, psoriasis, rosacea, skin cancer; caries, tooth loss, oral cancer; tinnitus, vertigo, sinusitis; refractive error, diabetic retinopathy, dry eye. Where the two overlap (sunscreen, retinoids, periodontitis, AMD, AREDS2, hearing→dementia, cataract→dementia) this file cross-references rather than repeats. The brain/cognition agent (Section 08) still owns the dementia endpoints; sleep apnea’s full cardiometabolic story lives in Section 22; allergy/immunology in Section 15.

These are the surfaces and sensors — the organs you see in the mirror and the four senses (sight, hearing, balance, smell/taste) that mediate every waking moment. They share a structure that makes them ideal for an honesty-graded manual:

  • The interventions that work are unglamorous and cheap (fluoride, sunscreen, a retinoid, an Epley maneuver, outdoor time for kids, a hearing aid) and the ones that sell are mostly theater (charcoal toothpaste, oil pulling, $300 serums, “eye exercises” for myopia, amalgam-removal “detox”).
  • Several have a hard mortality or function tail that earns them a place in a longevity manual: melanoma kills, oral cancer kills, untreated glaucoma blinds silently, sleep apnea drives cardiovascular disease, and vision/hearing loss now sit on the Lancet modifiable-dementia list (Section 11 §4.4, §5).
  • They are the cleanest test of the three honesty rules (06-evidence/SCHEMA.md): predictor ≠ lever (intraocular pressure predicts glaucoma; lowering it is a separately proven lever — and here it actually is); cohort ≠ RCT (charcoal “whitens” by abrasion in lab assays, not in outcome trials); something beats nothing (a $2 fluoride tube outperforms the entire “holistic dentistry” aisle).

One-line verdict up front: the best-evidenced moves in this entire section are fluoride (the single most cost-effective preventive intervention in dentistry), topical retinoids + sunscreen (Section 11 — the two best-evidenced skin actives), the Epley maneuver (a 60-second physical maneuver that cures the most common vertigo), outdoor time for children (the one myopia lever with RCT support), anti-VEGF injections (turned wet AMD from a blinding disease into a treatable one), and getting hearing and vision corrected (function + plausible dementia tail). Almost everything marketed around these — and most of the “wellness” reframes of dentistry and eye care — is theater.

Part A — DERMATOLOGY (the named skin diseases)

Section 11 §1 established the anti-aging skin story: ~80% of visible facial aging is UV-driven, and the two best-evidenced products on the shelf are sunscreen (RCT: photoaging + SCC + melanoma — Hughes 2013, Green 1999/2011) and topical retinoids (RCT: Weiss 1988). This part covers the inflammatory and neoplastic skin diseases people actually see a dermatologist for.

A.1 Acne vulgaris — what actually works, and the honest diet link

Acne is a disease of the pilosebaceous unit, driven by four interacting factors: (1) follicular hyperkeratinization (a plugged pore/comedo), (2) androgen-driven sebum overproduction, (3) Cutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes) proliferation, and (4) inflammation. Treatment works by hitting these nodes — and the evidence ladder is unusually clear.

Treatment Mechanism Best evidence Verdict
Topical retinoid (adapalene, tretinoin) Normalizes keratinization, anti-comedonal, anti-inflammatory meta (NMA) — core of every guideline First-line for almost all acne; adapalene is OTC and best-tolerated
Benzoyl peroxide (BPO) Bactericidal (oxidizes C. acnes), comedolytic; no resistance meta / rct Cheap, OTC, prevents antibiotic resistance — pair with everything
Topical antibiotic (clindamycin) — always with BPO Anti-C. acnes, anti-inflammatory meta Effective but never as monotherapy (resistance); fixed-combo with BPO/retinoid
Combination topical (retinoid + BPO ± antibiotic) Multi-node meta (NMA: best topical efficacy) The evidence-winning topical strategy
Oral antibiotic (doxycycline) Anti-inflammatory + anti-bacterial meta Moderate–severe; time-limited (~3 mo), always with topical BPO/retinoid
Combined oral contraceptive / spironolactone Anti-androgen meta / rct Effective in women; hormonal acne
Oral isotretinoin Shrinks sebaceous glands (only drug that hits all 4 factors) meta / rct The closest thing to a cure for severe/nodulocystic/scarring acne; teratogenic — pregnancy-prevention program mandatory
  • Network meta-analysis: the 2022 Br J Dermatol NMA of topical, oral, physical, and combined acne treatments (10.1111/bjd.21739) confirms combination topicals (retinoid + BPO ± antibiotic) lead on efficacy, and that oral isotretinoin is the most effective single agent for severe disease. meta.
  • Benzoyl peroxide: systematic review (10.3109/09546634.2012.699179) — effective, cheap, OTC, and critically does not induce bacterial resistance, which is why guidelines insist BPO accompany any antibiotic. meta.
  • Isotretinoin: systematic review (10.1111/bjd.15668) — high efficacy with durable remission; the famous harms (teratogenicity, mucocutaneous dryness, lab monitoring; the depression/IBD signals are not robustly causal in controlled analyses). meta / rct.
  • Guideline anchor: AAD 2024 acne guidelines (10.1016/j.jaad.2023.12.017).

The honest diet link. For decades dermatology said “diet doesn’t cause acne.” The honest 2020s position is narrower and more interesting: (1) high-glycemic-load diets modestly worsen acne (rct/cohort — plausible via insulin/IGF-1 → androgen/sebum signaling); (2) skim/low-fat milk shows a consistent association (cohort); (3) chocolate and greasy food per se remain unproven. The defensible synthesis: diet is a minor, real modifier in some people (low-GL eating is a reasonable adjunct), not the cause and not a substitute for retinoids/BPO. Honesty rule #1 — the dietary signal is a cohort/small-rct modifier, not the lever that clears moderate–severe acne.

A.2 Atopic dermatitis (eczema) — barrier + immune disease, and the biologic era

Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a chronic, relapsing, intensely itchy inflammatory disease driven by a two-hit model: a skin-barrier defect (filaggrin-gene loss-of-function mutations are the strongest genetic risk) plus type-2 immune (Th2) inflammation (IL-4, IL-13). The barrier defect lets allergens/irritants in; the immune response inflames; scratching breaks the barrier further — the “itch–scratch cycle.”

Tier Intervention Evidence Note
Foundation Emollients / moisturizers + gentle skincare meta / rct Repairs barrier; reduces flares and steroid need — the unglamorous backbone
First-line flare Topical corticosteroids (potency-matched) meta Mainstay; “steroid phobia” causes undertreatment — short bursts are safe
Steroid-sparing topical Calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus), crisaborole, topical JAK (ruxolitinib) rct For face/folds and maintenance
Moderate–severe systemic Dupilumab (anti-IL-4Rα) rct (SOLO 1/2) Transformed severe AD; targets the Th2 axis directly
Moderate–severe systemic Oral JAK inhibitors (upadacitinib, abrocitinib) rct Fast, potent; class-warning monitoring
  • Dupilumab — the landmark: Simpson 2016, NEJM (SOLO 1 & 2) (10.1056/NEJMoa1610020) — two phase-3 RCTs showed dupilumab dramatically improved moderate-to-severe AD vs placebo (EASI-75, itch, quality of life), with a clean safety profile (notable: conjunctivitis). rct / outcome. This was the proof that targeting type-2 cytokines controls severe eczema, and it opened the biologic era in dermatology beyond psoriasis.

Honest take: the foundation is boring and works — moisturize relentlessly, treat flares early with adequate (not homeopathic) topical steroid, avoid your triggers. “Steroid phobia” and chasing elimination diets cause more suffering than the steroids do. The biologics/JAKs are genuine breakthroughs but are for moderate–severe disease, not first-line for mild eczema. Bleach baths and “leaky gut” cures are mostly overhyped.

A.3 Psoriasis — an autoimmune disease, and one of biology’s cleanest drug-target stories

Psoriasis is a systemic immune-mediated disease, not a cosmetic “dry skin” problem. The mechanism is now precisely mapped: the IL-23 → Th17 → IL-17 axis drives keratinocyte hyperproliferation (the silvery scaly plaques) and is systemic — psoriasis carries excess risk of psoriatic arthritis (~20–30%), cardiovascular disease, and metabolic syndrome (Section 24 owns the joint disease).

Tier Intervention Evidence Note
Mild / limited Topical corticosteroids + vitamin-D analogue (calcipotriol) meta First-line for limited plaque psoriasis
Moderate–severe Phototherapy (narrowband UVB) rct Effective, no systemic immunosuppression
Moderate–severe systemic Methotrexate, ciclosporin, apremilast, acitretin meta Conventional systemics; cheaper, less effective than biologics
Moderate–severe biologic Anti-IL-17 (secukinumab, ixekizumab, bimekizumab), anti-IL-23 (risankizumab, guselkumab), anti-TNF meta (NMA) The IL-17/IL-23 biologics top the efficacy rankings — many patients reach clear/almost-clear skin (PASI 90–100)
  • The definitive comparison: Sbidian 2023, Cochrane NMA (10.1002/14651858.CD011535.pub6, latest of a serially-updated review) — a network meta-analysis of systemic psoriasis treatments finds the anti-IL-17 and anti-IL-23 biologics (with bimekizumab, ixekizumab, risankizumab, secukinumab, guselkumab among the top) achieve the highest rates of PASI 90 vs placebo and outperform older systemics. meta / outcome. This is one of the cleanest bench-to-clinic stories in medicine: the cytokine mechanism was mapped, drugs were built against the exact node, and they work.

Honest take: psoriasis is treatable to near-clearance for most people now — that is a genuine modern win. The honest caveats: biologics are immunosuppressants (infection screening, cost), and none is a cure (stopping relapses). “Anti-inflammatory diets,” supplements, and detoxes do not control moderate-to-severe psoriasis; the disease is immune, and the immune-targeted drugs are what move it.

A.4 Rosacea — chronic facial inflammation, not “adult acne”

Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory facial condition (central-face erythema, flushing, papules/pustules, telangiectasias, and — in some — phymatous skin thickening and ocular involvement). Mechanism is multifactorial: dysregulated innate immunity (cathelicidin/LL-37), neurovascular hyperreactivity, and the Demodex mite/its microbiome. It is not acne (no comedones) and not curable, but it is controllable.

Subtype/feature First-line Evidence
Persistent erythema Topical brimonidine / oxymetazoline (vasoconstrictors); laser/IPL for telangiectasias rct
Papulopustular Topical metronidazole, azelaic acid, ivermectin; oral doxycycline (sub-antimicrobial 40 mg) meta (Cochrane)
Refractory/phymatous Low-dose oral isotretinoin; surgical/laser for rhinophyma meta
Trigger control Avoid sun, heat, alcohol, spicy food, stress (individualized) cohort
  • Cochrane: van Zuuren 2015, Br J Dermatol (abridged Cochrane with GRADE, 10.1111/bjd.13956) — best evidence supports topical ivermectin, azelaic acid, brimonidine, and doxycycline; many older treatments are weakly supported. meta.
  • Low-dose isotretinoin: 2025 JEADV systematic review/meta (10.1111/jdv.20315) — effective for refractory rosacea. meta.

Honest take: rosacea is managed, not cured — daily sun protection plus a proven topical (ivermectin/azelaic acid) is the backbone, and sub-antimicrobial-dose doxycycline (anti-inflammatory, not antibiotic dosing) is the oral workhorse. “Rosacea diets” and elaborate skincare routines mostly help by removing irritants; the active ingredients above are what reduce lesions.

A.5 Skin cancer — the one dermatology category that kills (cross-ref Section 11 §1, Section 25 oncology)

Three cancers dominate, in ascending lethality:

Cancer Frequency Behavior Key facts
Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) Most common cancer in humans Locally destructive, almost never metastasizes Pearly papule, rolled border, telangiectasias; cured by excision/Mohs; sun-driven
Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) 2nd most common Can metastasize (low but real); precursor = actinic keratosis Scaly/crusted/ulcerated; sun + immunosuppression; sunscreen reduces it (RCT — Green 1999)
Melanoma ~1% of skin cancers, most skin-cancer deaths Aggressive, metastasizes early; survival is stage-dependent Early = curable by excision; advanced = the disease that checkpoint inhibitors transformed (Section 25)
  • ABCDE rule (melanoma screening): Abbasi 2004, JAMA (10.1001/jama.292.22.2771) — the consensus early-detection criteria: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variegation, Diameter >6 mm, Evolving (the most important — change over time). Plus the “ugly duckling” sign (a mole that looks unlike its neighbors). consensus/diagnostic. Self-skin-checks and dermatologist exams (especially with a prior melanoma, many atypical nevi, family history, or fair skin/red hair) catch it early, when excision cures.
  • Prevention = the Section 11 sunscreen + tanning-bed story: Green 1999 (SCC↓, rct), Green 2011 (melanoma↓ ~50% at 10 yr, rct-derived), Ghiasvand 2016 (tanning beds↑ melanoma, cohort). Sun protection is the only proven primary-prevention lever.
  • Melanoma systemic therapy (advanced disease) — checkpoint immunotherapy and BRAF/MEK targeted therapy — lives in Section 25 (oncology).

Honest take: the lethality gradient is the whole point — BCC almost never kills, melanoma routinely does, and the difference is caught with your eyes. A changing/new/ugly-duckling lesion is worth a dermatologist visit; the ABCDE/ugly-duckling heuristics are imperfect but high-leverage. Mole-mapping apps and AI dermoscopy are improving but not yet a substitute for a biopsy of a suspicious lesion.

A.6 The honest skincare-industry take (extends Section 11 §1.5)

Section 11’s hierarchy stands: sunscreen + retinoid are tier-1, moisturizer is tier-2-real-but-cosmetic, and most serums are marketing. Adding the actives with some real evidence beyond those two:

Active Evidence Honest verdict
Sunscreen (broad-spectrum) rct (photoaging, SCC, melanoma) Tier 1 — the single best-evidenced product
Topical retinoid (tretinoin > retinol) rct Tier 1 — best-evidenced active; slow, irritating, must continue
Vitamin C (L-ascorbic acid, properly formulated) small rct / mechanistic Modest antioxidant/brightening; formulation-sensitive (oxidizes); real-but-minor
Niacinamide small rct Modest barrier/tone/oil benefits; well-tolerated; real-but-minor
Alpha-hydroxy acids (glycolic, lactic) rct Real exfoliation/texture benefit
Azelaic acid rct (acne, rosacea, pigment) A genuine multi-use active
Hyaluronic acid / ceramides (moisturizers) rct (hydration) Real but cosmetic/transient (the Section 11 tier-2 point)
Peptides, growth factors, “stem cell,” exosomes, most “firming” weak / mechanistic Marketing outruns evidence
Price as a quality signal — No correlation between price and efficacy; a $12 drugstore retinoid/sunscreen beats a $300 serum with neither

The one-line industry truth: the active ingredients that work are cheap, generic, and decades old. The premium you pay above a competent drugstore sunscreen + retinoid + moisturizer buys packaging, scent, and texture, not better skin. (Honesty rule #1 throughout: most serum claims are mechanistic/invitro, sold as if they were outcome.)

Part B — DENTAL & ORAL (the most-skipped organ, beyond periodontal)

Section 11 §2 owns the periodontal–systemic story (periodontitis ↔︎ CVD/diabetes/dementia; the one proven systemic lever is scaling lowering HbA1c — Simpson 2022 Cochrane; the P. gingivalis/Alzheimer’s lead — Dominy 2019; the flossing-evidence honesty note — Sambunjak 2011). This part covers the rest of dentistry: caries (the most common chronic disease on Earth), tooth loss, oral cancer, and the honest take on “holistic dentistry.”

B.1 Dental caries — the actual cause, and the fluoride evidence

Caries (tooth decay) is not “sugar rotting teeth” in the naive sense and not a vitamin deficiency. The real mechanism is a dysbiotic biofilm acid attack:

  1. Biofilm (dental plaque) — acid-producing bacteria (Streptococcus mutans, Lactobacilli) colonize the tooth surface.
  2. Fermentable sugar (especially frequency, not just amount) — the bacteria metabolize it to organic acids.
  3. Acid demineralizes enamel (drops local pH below ~5.5, dissolving hydroxyapatite).
  4. Saliva + fluoride remineralize between acid attacks — caries is the net balance of demin vs remin over time. Decay happens when demineralization chronically outpaces remineralization.

This model explains everything practical: it is frequency of sugar exposure (sipping soda all day, constant snacking) that drives decay more than total quantity; saliva is protective (dry mouth → rampant caries); and fluoride works by shifting the remineralization balance (forms fluorapatite, more acid-resistant; also antibacterial).

  • Fluoride toothpaste — the foundational evidence: Marinho 2003, Cochrane (10.1002/14651858.CD002278) — fluoride toothpaste vs placebo gives a clear caries reduction in children (prevented-fraction ~24% on the DMFS index). meta / outcome. This is one of the best-evidenced preventive interventions in all of medicine.
  • Concentration matters: Walsh 2019, Cochrane (10.1002/14651858.CD007868.pub3) — higher fluoride concentrations (≥1000 ppm) prevent more caries; the benefit is dose-dependent, and 1000–1500 ppm is the standard adult range. meta.
  • Water fluoridation & topical fluoride (varnish, mouthrinse) add further, smaller, independently-evidenced benefits. Community water fluoridation is one of the CDC’s “10 great public-health achievements of the 20th century” — though the modern marginal benefit is smaller now that fluoride toothpaste is near-universal.

Honest take: the highest-leverage caries levers are (1) fluoride toothpaste, twice daily (“spit, don’t rinse” — leaving a thin fluoride film is the point), (2) reduce sugar frequency (not just amount), and (3) regular professional care (sealants for kids’ molars have strong RCT support). Flossing’s direct caries evidence is weak (the Section 11 honesty note: bad trials, not a useless practice), but interdental cleaning is mechanistically sound for the interproximal surfaces a brush can’t reach.

B.2 Periodontal (gum) disease — cross-ref Section 11 §2

Gum disease is a spectrum from gingivitis (reversible inflammation, bleeding gums — plaque-driven) to periodontitis (irreversible destruction of the bone and ligament holding teeth, the leading cause of adult tooth loss). The full story — including the systemic associations and the one RCT-proven systemic lever (scaling → HbA1c↓ in diabetics) — is in Section 11 §2. The practical action repeated here: brush twice daily with fluoride, clean between teeth daily, and see a hygienist — professional scaling/root planing is the intervention with the actual RCT support.

  • Interdental cleaning: Worthington 2019, Cochrane (10.1002/14651858.CD012018.pub2) — interdental brushes/ floss/water flossers added to brushing reduce gingivitis (low-to-moderate certainty); interdental brushes have somewhat better evidence than string floss where gaps allow. meta. Same honest framing as Section 11: the trials are weak, the practice is biologically sensible and low-risk.

B.3 Tooth loss & dentures — function, nutrition, and a dignity issue

Tooth loss (edentulism) is the downstream failure of caries + periodontitis, and it is more than cosmetic: fewer functional teeth associates with poorer diet quality (people avoid hard/fibrous foods → less produce, more soft processed food), and edentulism associates with frailty, cognitive decline, and mortality in cohort data (cohort — confounded by socioeconomic status and shared risk factors; predictor more than proven lever).

Replacement option What Note
Dental implants Titanium root + crown Highest function/satisfaction; bone-preserving; cost/surgery the barrier
Fixed bridge Crowns spanning a gap Good function; relies on adjacent teeth
Removable partial/complete dentures Prosthetic teeth Most accessible; lower chewing efficiency; need relines as bone resorbs

Honest take: keeping your own teeth (prevention above) beats every replacement. When teeth are lost, implants restore the most function but cost gates access; dentures are a real, dignity-preserving option. The under-appreciated point is nutritional — restoring chewing function in an older adult is a quiet quality-of-diet (and therefore healthspan) intervention.

B.4 Oral cancer — the deadly one dentists screen for

Oral and oropharyngeal cancers (mostly squamous cell carcinoma) are the lethal tail of mouth disease — often caught late, with ~50–60% 5-year survival overall (much better when caught early). Two distinct causal stories:

Driver Cancer pattern Trend
Tobacco (all forms) + alcohol (synergistic) Classic oral-cavity SCC (tongue, floor of mouth, gingiva) Declining with smoking rates
HPV (high-risk, esp. type 16) Oropharyngeal SCC (tonsil, base of tongue) Rising — now the dominant cause of oropharyngeal cancer in many high-income countries; better prognosis than HPV-negative; HPV vaccination is primary prevention
Betel/areca nut, sun (lip), immunosuppression, chronic inflammation Various Region-dependent

Honest take: the levers are don’t smoke/chew tobacco, moderate alcohol, get HPV-vaccinated, and let your dentist do the oral-cancer screen (the visual/palpation exam at checkups — the practical reason routine dental visits matter beyond cleaning). Any non-healing mouth ulcer, red/white patch (erythroplakia/leukoplakia), or lump lasting >2–3 weeks warrants evaluation. The HPV-vaccine → oropharyngeal-cancer-prevention link is a genuine modern prevention win (cross-ref Section 25/26).

B.5 The honest take on “holistic dentistry,” charcoal, oil-pulling, whitening, and amalgam fear

This is the section’s densest honesty cluster — a wellness-marketing minefield over a field with strong real evidence.

Claim Reality Grade
Charcoal toothpaste “detoxifies / whitens” Whitens only by abrasion (it’s a mild scrub); no detox mechanism; high abrasivity can wear enamel; usually no fluoride (so it forgoes the one proven benefit). No RCT of caries/whitening outcomes. mechanistic/marketing — net-negative if it replaces fluoride toothpaste
Oil pulling (swishing coconut/sesame oil) Systematic reviews find at best weak, low-quality evidence vs chlorhexidine/standard care; any plaque effect is small and unreplicated; harmless but not a substitute for brushing/fluoride; lipoid pneumonia if aspirated (rare). meta (low quality) — 10.1016/j.heliyon.2020.e04789 — overhyped
Whitening (peroxide strips/gels, in-office) Actually works — peroxide genuinely bleaches via oxidation; this is the one cosmetic that does what it says. Sensitivity is the main side effect; doesn’t damage enamel at proper concentrations. rct — legit
“Holistic / biological dentistry” A spectrum: the good parts (minimally-invasive dentistry, prevention focus) are mainstream; the bad parts (routine amalgam removal for “detox,” “cavitation surgery,” fluoride-rejection, “meridian tooth charts”) range from unproven to harmful. mixed — fluoride-rejection is the red flag
“Silver (amalgam) fillings poison you with mercury” Dental amalgam releases trace mercury vapor, but at levels far below any toxicity threshold for the general population; large reviews and the FDA/WHO/ADA find no evidence of systemic harm in people with amalgams. Removing sound amalgams “to detox” actually spikes mercury exposure during drilling — net-harmful. (Composite resins are now often preferred for aesthetic/conservative reasons, not safety — and Cochrane finds composites have a higher failure/recurrent-caries rate than amalgam in load-bearing posterior teeth.) meta — 10.1002/14651858.CD005620.pub3 — the fear is unfounded; removal-for-detox is the actual harm

Honest take: dentistry has excellent cheap evidence-based tools (fluoride, sealants, scaling, professional whitening) and a large wellness-marketing shadow that mostly sells people away from the one intervention (fluoride) that has the strongest evidence. The single highest-value filter: anything that tells you to stop using fluoride or to rip out sound fillings to “detox” is selling fear, not health.

Part C — ENT (Ear, Nose, Throat — the senses of hearing and balance)

Section 11 §5 owns the hearing→cognition story (the ACHIEVE trial — Lin 2023; untreated hearing loss on the Lancet dementia list; the noise-protection levers). This part covers the named ENT conditions: tinnitus, vertigo/BPPV, sinusitis, and the ENT view of sleep apnea.

C.1 Hearing loss — clinical detail (cross-ref Section 11 §5, Section 08 brain)

Two mechanistic categories with very different treatments:

Type Cause Treatment
Sensorineural (most common, usually permanent) Cochlear hair-cell/nerve damage — age (presbycusis), noise, ototoxic drugs, genetics Hearing aids (incl. OTC since 2022); cochlear implants for severe-profound
Conductive (often fixable) Sound blocked before the cochlea — cerumen (wax) impaction, otitis media/effusion, otosclerosis, perforation Treat the cause (wax removal, tubes, stapedectomy)
Mixed Both Both

The cognition handoff (ACHIEVE: hearing aids slowed decline ~48% in the higher-risk subgroup — 10.1016/ S0140-6736(23)01406-X) and the noise-protection levers (85 dB action threshold, +3 dB halves safe time, 60/60 earbud rule) are in Section 11 §5. The clinical addition here: don’t dismiss treatable conductive causes (a wax plug or middle-ear effusion is reversible), test hearing in midlife, and adopt aids early — the years-long neural-adaptation period plus the ACHIEVE signal both argue against “waiting until it’s bad.”

C.2 Tinnitus — the honest “no cure, but treatable suffering” story

Tinnitus is the perception of sound without an external source (ringing, buzzing, hissing) — a symptom, not a disease, affecting ~10–15% of adults. Mechanism: most commonly it arises from maladaptive central plasticity following cochlear damage — the brain “turns up the gain” on missing input (often paired with hearing loss), a phantom-sensation analogous to phantom-limb pain (cross-ref Section 21 central sensitization).

The honest core fact: there is no proven drug or device that eliminates tinnitus. What works is reducing the distress and attention the sound commands — the goal is habituation, not silence.

Approach What it does Evidence
CBT (cognitive behavioural therapy) Reduces tinnitus-related distress, anxiety, quality-of-life impact (does not change loudness) meta (Cochrane) — the best-evidenced intervention
Hearing aids (if hearing loss present) Amplify ambient sound → less contrast with the tinnitus; often markedly helpful rct/cohort
Sound therapy / maskers / TRT Background sound + counseling to promote habituation rct (modest/mixed)
Treat reversible contributors Wax, ototoxic meds, hearing loss, sometimes anxiety/insomnia clinical
Supplements (ginkgo, zinc, melatonin), “tinnitus cures” online No reliable benefit; melatonin may help associated insomnia meta (null/weak) — avoid the scams
  • CBT evidence: Fuller 2020, Cochrane (10.1002/14651858.CD012614.pub2) — CBT improves tinnitus-related quality of life and reduces depression/anxiety, with little/no effect on subjective loudness. meta / outcome. The honest framing in one finding: you treat the suffering, not the sound.

Honest take: anyone selling a tinnitus “cure” (a pill, a supplement, a frequency app that erases it) is selling to desperate people. The legitimate path is treat any hearing loss, address reversible causes, and use CBT/sound therapy to habituate — most people’s tinnitus becomes far less intrusive over time even though the signal persists. Sudden unilateral tinnitus, or tinnitus with hearing loss/vertigo, needs prompt ENT evaluation (rule out treatable/serious causes).

C.3 Vertigo & BPPV — where a 60-second maneuver actually cures the disease

“Dizziness” is a wastebasket; the high-yield distinction is vertigo (a false sense of spinning/movement, usually an inner-ear/vestibular problem) vs presyncope/disequilibrium. The single most important fact in this whole section’s “things that work” column:

  • Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV) — the most common cause of vertigo — is caused by displaced otoconia (calcium-carbonate “ear rocks”) drifting into a semicircular canal, where they make the canal falsely signal motion with head position changes. It is mechanical, benign, and physically curable by repositioning the crystals back out of the canal.

  • The Epley maneuver (canalith repositioning) — a sequence of timed head/body positions — physically rolls the otoconia out of the posterior canal. It is a ~60-second bedside procedure that resolves BPPV in a single session in the majority of cases.

  • Evidence: Hilton & Pinder, Cochrane (10.1002/14651858.CD003162) — the Epley maneuver is effective for posterior-canal BPPV (higher resolution of vertigo and negative Dix-Hallpike vs sham/control). meta / outcome. Confirmed by the AAO-HNS systematic reviews (10.1177/0194599814527732). This is one of the cleanest “the treatment works and it’s free” facts in clinical medicine.

Honest take: BPPV is diagnosable with one bedside test (Dix-Hallpike) and curable with one maneuver (Epley) — no drugs, no surgery, no supplements. Vestibular suppressant drugs (meclizine) only mask symptoms and delay recovery; they are not the treatment. Other vertigo causes (vestibular neuritis, Ménière’s disease, vestibular migraine, and the can’t-miss central causes — stroke/posterior-circulation) need their own work-up; persistent, spontaneous, or neurologically-accompanied vertigo is not BPPV and needs evaluation.

C.4 Sinusitis — the over-antibiotic’d infection

Rhinosinusitis (inflammation of the nose + paranasal sinuses) is mostly a self-limiting viral illness mislabeled and over-treated. The honest grading:

Type Cause Treatment
Acute viral (most cases <10 days) Common cold viruses Supportive — saline irrigation, analgesia, time; antibiotics do not help
Acute bacterial (minority) Suggested by >10 days without improvement, “double-worsening,” high fever + purulence Antibiotics may help a subset; many still resolve without
Chronic rhinosinusitis (>12 weeks) Inflammatory ± polyps, allergy, biofilm Intranasal corticosteroids, saline irrigation, allergy management; surgery (FESS) or biologics (anti-IL-4/5) for refractory

Honest take: most “sinus infections” are viral and antibiotics are useless for them (a major source of antibiotic overuse and resistance — cross-ref Section 26). The evidence-based levers are saline irrigation and intranasal corticosteroids; antibiotics are reserved for genuine bacterial cases. Chronic sinusitis is an inflammatory disease and is managed like one (steroids, not repeated antibiotic courses).

C.5 Sleep apnea — the ENT/sleep overlap (cross-ref Section 22, Section 11)

Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) — repetitive upper-airway collapse during sleep causing intermittent hypoxia and fragmentation — sits at the ENT/sleep/cardiometabolic intersection. Its full cardiometabolic and cognitive story is in Section 22; the honest summary relevant here:

  • CPAP unambiguously fixes the symptoms (daytime sleepiness, quality of life, blood pressure modestly, bed-partner sleep) — these are robust rct benefits.
  • CPAP’s hard cardiovascular-event benefit is NOT proven in RCTs: McEvoy 2016, NEJM (SAVE) (10.1056/NEJMoa1606599) — CPAP did not reduce cardiovascular events vs usual care in people with OSA + known CVD. rct / outcome (a null). The honest catch: adherence was low (~3.3 h/night), and observational/meta analyses (10.1001/jama.2023.17465) suggest good adherence (≥4 h) may reduce events — so the null is confounded by under-use, not necessarily a true absence of benefit. Predictor-vs-lever and dose-matters honesty rules both bite here.

Honest take: treat OSA for the symptoms and quality of life — that benefit is real and large. Treating it specifically to prevent heart attacks rests on weaker (adherence-confounded) evidence. CPAP is first-line; oral appliances, weight loss (often curative in mild OSA), positional therapy, and selected surgery are alternatives.

Part D — OPHTHALMOLOGY (the named eye diseases)

Section 11 §4 owns the longevity-lever eye story (AMD + the AREDS2 supplement win; cataract→dementia — Lee 2022; glaucoma screening — USPSTF; vision→dementia — Livingston 2024; the screens/myopia summary). This part covers the clinical eye diseases and treatments, plus the honest “eye exercises” debunk.

D.1 Refractive error & the myopia epidemic — the one childhood lever that’s RCT-proven

Refractive error (myopia/near-sightedness, hyperopia/far-sightedness, astigmatism, presbyopia) is the most common visual problem — the eye’s optics don’t focus light on the retina. It is corrected (glasses, contacts, LASIK/PRK refractive surgery), not “cured.” The important public-health story is the myopia epidemic:

  • Myopia prevalence has risen dramatically, especially in East Asia (up to ~80–90% of young adults in some urban populations), driven by a gene–environment mismatch. The mechanism: insufficient time outdoors during childhood → less bright-light exposure → less retinal dopamine → unchecked axial elongation of the eyeball. (Near-work contributes, but “screens” specifically are a weaker/confounded signal than lack of outdoor light.)
  • The RCT-proven lever — outdoor time: He 2015, JAMA (10.1001/jama.2015.10803) — a cluster-RCT in Guangzhou added 40 minutes of outdoor class time per school day; over 3 years it reduced the incidence of new myopia vs control schools. rct / outcome. Replicated by later objectively-monitored outdoor-time RCTs (10.1016/j.ophtha.2022.06.024) and meta-analysis (10.1111/aos.13403). This is the one primary-prevention lever for childhood myopia with randomized support.
  • Slowing progression in already-myopic kids: low-dose atropine eye drops, orthokeratology, and myopia-control contact/spectacle lenses have RCT support for slowing axial elongation. (Treating progression matters because high myopia raises lifelong risk of retinal detachment, myopic maculopathy, and glaucoma.)

Honest take: get children outside (~2 hours/day) — it’s the cheapest, best-evidenced myopia-prevention lever, and it works via light, not “looking far away.” For progression, atropine/ortho-K/control lenses are real. For adults, glasses/contacts/refractive surgery correct the optics; there is no exercise or training that reverses refractive error (see §D.7).

D.2 Cataract — the most common surgery in medicine (cross-ref Section 11 §4.2)

A cataract is clouding of the eye’s natural lens (progressive protein aggregation/oxidation with age) — the leading cause of reversible blindness worldwide. The fix is phacoemulsification + intraocular lens implant: the clouded lens is emulsified and replaced with a clear artificial one. It is one of the most common, safest, and most effective elective operations performed (millions/year, ~15-minute outpatient procedure, high success).

  • The cataract→dementia finding (Lee 2022, 10.1001/jamainternmed.2021.6990 — extraction associated with ~30% lower dementia risk, with glaucoma surgery as a negative control) is in Section 11 §4.2. The clinical point here: cataract surgery is definitively curative for the vision loss and remarkably low-risk; the only honest caveat is timing (operate when the cataract impairs function/quality of life, not on a number).

Honest take: there is no eye drop, supplement, or exercise that reverses an established cataract (some drops are marketed; none works). The treatment is surgery, and it is excellent.

D.3 Glaucoma — the silent thief, and the one node we can actually lower

Glaucoma is a group of progressive optic neuropathies — death of retinal ganglion cells/optic-nerve fibers — that causes irreversible, painless, peripheral-first vision loss (you don’t notice until central/late). The biggest modifiable risk factor is elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), though glaucoma occurs at normal pressure too. It is the “silent thief of sight” — and the second-leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide.

  • The lever IS proven — lowering IOP works: Heijl 2002, Arch Ophthalmol — Early Manifest Glaucoma Trial (EMGT) (10.1001/archopht.120.10.1268) — randomly lowering IOP (laser + topical drug) in newly-detected open-angle glaucoma slowed progression vs no initial treatment (progression 45% treated vs 62% control). rct / outcome. Unusually for this section, IOP is both a predictor AND a proven lever — lowering it (drops, laser/SLT, surgery) preserves vision in detected cases. This is exactly why the USPSTF “insufficient evidence for mass screening” statement (Section 11 §4.3) does not mean “glaucoma can’t be treated” — once detected, treatment works; the unproven link is the population-screening-program → outcome chain.
Type Mechanism Note
Primary open-angle (most common) Gradual outflow resistance ↑; painless, chronic Treated with IOP-lowering drops/SLT laser/surgery
Angle-closure (acute) Sudden drainage-angle blockage → IOP spikes Emergency — pain, red eye, halos, nausea; can blind fast
Normal-tension Ganglion-cell loss at “normal” IOP Still benefits from further IOP lowering

Honest take: glaucoma is the strongest case for risk-based eye exams (age, family history, African/Hispanic ancestry, high IOP, high myopia) — because it’s symptomless until vision is permanently gone, and because once caught, IOP-lowering genuinely preserves sight (EMGT). Lost vision can’t be recovered, so detection is everything. No supplement, diet, or “eye exercise” treats glaucoma.

D.4 Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) — AREDS2 + the anti-VEGF revolution

AMD degrades the macula (central, high-acuity retina) — the leading cause of central vision loss in older adults. Two forms:

Form Mechanism Treatment
Dry (atrophic) — ~85–90% Drusen accumulation → gradual RPE/photoreceptor atrophy (geographic atrophy late) AREDS2 supplements slow progression in intermediate AMD (Section 11 §4.1); new complement inhibitors (pegcetacoplan) modestly slow geographic atrophy
Wet (neovascular) — ~10–15%, most rapid vision loss Abnormal choroidal neovascularization leaking under the retina Anti-VEGF intravitreal injections — transformed it from a blinding disease to a treatable one
  • AREDS2 (the supplement win): AREDS2 2013, JAMA (10.1001/jama.2013.4997) — full detail in Section 11 §4.1; works only for intermediate or unilateral-advanced AMD, not prevention. rct.
  • Anti-VEGF — the modern revolution: Rosenfeld 2006, NEJM (MARINA) (10.1056/NEJMoa054481) — monthly intravitreal ranibizumab for neovascular AMD not only prevented vision loss but improved vision in a substantial fraction (~95% lost <15 letters; ~34% gained ≥15 letters) vs sham. rct / outcome. Anti-VEGF agents (ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab off-label, faricimab) are now the standard of care — one of the biggest treatment advances in modern ophthalmology, converting wet AMD from near-certain central-vision loss to a manageable chronic condition.

Honest take: wet AMD is now treatable (anti-VEGF) — urgently (sudden central distortion/scotoma = same-week ophthalmology). Dry AMD is slowed (not reversed) by AREDS2 only in the right stage; the new GA drugs are modest. Prevention overlaps with cardiovascular health (don’t smoke — smoking is the strongest modifiable AMD risk factor).

D.5 Diabetic retinopathy — the preventable blinding complication

Diabetic retinopathy is microvascular damage to the retina from chronic hyperglycemia — a leading cause of blindness in working-age adults, and largely preventable by glycemic/blood-pressure control plus screening.

  • Glucose control prevents it: the DCCT (Diabetes Control and Complications Trial), NEJM 1993 (10.1056/NEJM199309303291401) — intensive glucose control in type 1 diabetes reduced the development and progression of retinopathy by 76%/54% vs conventional control. rct / outcome. (UKPDS showed the parallel in type 2.) Blood-pressure control adds further benefit.
  • Screening + treatment work: regular dilated retinal exams (or AI/photographic screening) catch it before symptoms; treatments — laser photocoagulation, anti-VEGF injections, and vitrectomy — preserve vision in detected disease. The progression is silent until advanced, so annual screening from diagnosis is the lever.

Honest take: diabetic retinopathy is a preventable, screenable cause of blindness — the levers are glucose control (DCCT), blood-pressure control, and never skipping the annual dilated eye exam. By the time vision blurs, damage is often advanced; the win is in screening + early treatment (cross-ref Section 22 diabetes).

D.6 Dry eye disease — common, real, and often mismanaged

Dry eye (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) is a chronic disease of the tear film and ocular surface — far more than “my eyes feel dry.” Mechanism: tear-film instability + hyperosmolarity → ocular-surface inflammation, most commonly from meibomian-gland dysfunction (MGD) (the oil layer fails → tears evaporate too fast) rather than pure aqueous deficiency. Worsened by screens (reduced blink rate), age, contact lenses, low humidity, and some systemic diseases (Sjögren’s).

Tier Intervention Note
Foundation Artificial tears, lid hygiene, warm compresses (for MGD), humidity, blink/screen breaks, omega-3 (mixed evidence) First-line
Anti-inflammatory Topical ciclosporin, lifitegrast, short steroid pulses For inflammatory/moderate disease
Procedural Punctal plugs, intense pulsed light/thermal MGD treatments, autologous serum tears (severe) Refractory
  • Framework: TFOS DEWS II 2017 (10.1016/j.jtos.2017.05.006 management; 10.1016/j.jtos.2017.05.008 definition) — the consensus reframing dry eye as a chronic inflammatory ocular-surface disease, mostly evaporative/MGD-driven, treated in a stepped fashion. consensus/meta.

Honest take: dry eye is real, common, and a treatable inflammatory disease — not just “use drops.” The highest-yield self-care is treating meibomian-gland dysfunction (warm compresses/lid hygiene), blinking fully during screen time (the digital-eye-strain overlap — Section 11 §4.5), and stepping up to anti-inflammatory drops when needed. The 20-20-20 habit manages the strain; it doesn’t cure the disease.

D.7 The honest “eye exercises / vision therapy for refractive error” debunk

The persistent wellness claim — popularized by the Bates method (1920s) and modern “improve your eyesight naturally” programs/apps — is that eye exercises, “palming,” focusing drills, or staring routines can reduce myopia and let you ditch your glasses. They cannot.

  • The mechanism rules it out: refractive error is a structural/optical property — the axial length of the eyeball and the cornea/lens optics. No muscular exercise changes the length of your eyeball or the curvature of your cornea. (The ciliary muscle changes lens accommodation for near focus, not the baseline refraction.)
  • The evidence rules it out: the American Academy of Ophthalmology position is explicit — no scientific evidence that eye exercises, vision training, or the Bates method improve or reverse refractive errors (myopia, hyperopia, astigmatism, presbyopia). Reviews of “behavioural vision therapy” for refractive error find no efficacy. meta/consensus (refutes).
  • The narrow legitimate exception: orthoptic vision therapy is genuinely effective for a specific binocular disorder — convergence insufficiency (the CITT RCT showed office-based vergence/accommodative therapy works). That is a real, evidence-based use of “eye exercises” — but it treats an eye-teaming problem, not refractive error. The marketing exploits this kernel of truth to oversell.

Honest take: eye exercises do not fix near/far-sightedness — that’s settled. The only proven myopia levers are outdoor time (prevention, kids) and atropine/ortho-K/control lenses (slowing progression) — none of them an “exercise.” Vision therapy is real only for binocular-vision disorders like convergence insufficiency. Anyone selling “throw away your glasses” through eye workouts is selling a century-old debunked claim.

The honest one-paragraph summary of this section

Across skin, mouth, ear, and eye, the pattern is the same and clean: the proven interventions are cheap, unglamorous, and mostly preventive — fluoride for caries (the best-evidenced tool in dentistry), sunscreen + a retinoid for skin, the Epley maneuver for the most common vertigo (a free 60-second cure), outdoor time to prevent childhood myopia, IOP-lowering for detected glaucoma, anti-VEGF for wet AMD, glucose control for diabetic retinopathy, and getting hearing/vision actually corrected (function plus a plausible dementia tail). The biologic era genuinely transformed three diseases — dupilumab for severe eczema, IL-17/IL-23 blockers for psoriasis, and anti-VEGF for wet AMD are real, RCT-proven wins. And the honesty rules bite hardest here against a thick layer of wellness theater: charcoal toothpaste and oil-pulling are net-negative-to-useless, amalgam-removal “detox” is the actual harm (the mercury fear is unfounded), $300 serums don’t beat a $12 retinoid, eye exercises do not fix refractive error (settled), tinnitus has no cure but real distress-treatment (CBT), CPAP fixes symptoms-but-not-proven-events, and most “sinus infections” don’t need antibiotics. The named diseases that kill or blind — melanoma, oral cancer, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, wet AMD — earn their place by being caught with your eyes, a dental exam, or a screening visit, which is exactly why these surface-and-sensory specialties belong in a longevity manual.

Go deeper

  • Simpson EL, et al. Two Phase 3 Trials of Dupilumab versus Placebo in Atopic Dermatitis (SOLO 1 & 2). NEJM
    1. 10.1056/NEJMoa1610020 — the trial that opened the biologic era for severe eczema.
  • Sbidian E, et al. Systemic pharmacological treatments for chronic plaque psoriasis: a network meta-analysis. Cochrane 2023. 10.1002/14651858.CD011535.pub6 — IL-17/IL-23 biologics top the efficacy rankings; the clean bench-to-clinic story.
  • Abbasi NR, et al. Early diagnosis of cutaneous melanoma: revisiting the ABCD criteria. JAMA 2004. 10.1001/jama.292.22.2771 — the ABCDE early-detection consensus.
  • Marinho VCC, et al. Fluoride toothpastes for preventing dental caries in children and adolescents. Cochrane
    1. 10.1002/14651858.CD002278 (concentration: Walsh 2019, 10.1002/14651858.CD007868.pub3) — the foundational fluoride evidence.
  • Cochrane (Innes/Schwendicke). Composite resin vs amalgam fillings for posterior teeth. 2021. 10.1002/14651858.CD005620.pub3 — the basis for the honest amalgam-safety take.
  • Fuller T, et al. Cognitive behavioural therapy for tinnitus. Cochrane 2020. 10.1002/14651858.CD012614.pub2 — CBT treats the distress, not the loudness; the best-evidenced tinnitus intervention.
  • Hilton MP, Pinder DK. The Epley (canalith repositioning) manoeuvre for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. Cochrane. 10.1002/14651858.CD003162 — a 60-second maneuver that cures the most common vertigo.
  • McEvoy RD, et al. CPAP for Prevention of Cardiovascular Events in Obstructive Sleep Apnea (SAVE). NEJM 2016. 10.1056/NEJMoa1606599 — CPAP fixes symptoms; the hard-CV-event benefit is null-but-adherence-confounded.
  • He M, et al. Effect of Time Spent Outdoors at School on the Development of Myopia Among Children in China. JAMA 2015. 10.1001/jama.2015.10803 — the RCT-proven childhood-myopia prevention lever.
  • Heijl A, et al. Reduction of intraocular pressure and glaucoma progression: results from the Early Manifest Glaucoma Trial (EMGT). Arch Ophthalmol 2002. 10.1001/archopht.120.10.1268 — IOP is both predictor and proven lever; lowering it preserves sight.

Part V

34 — Emergency, Acute Care & First Aid

Manual section, v1.0 — 2026-06-28. Companion graded claims in 02-domains/emergency-claims.json. Every other section of this manual is about the long game — how to live well across decades. This one is about the next ten minutes. A complete map of human health has to include what kills acutely and what an ordinary person can actually do about it. Most premature deaths in the developed world are slow (cardiometabolic disease, cancer — Sections 22, 25). But a meaningful fraction are fast and reversible: a clot that stops a heart, a peanut that closes an airway, a bleed that empties a body, an opioid that stops a breath. In those minutes the most decisive medical intervention on Earth is not a hospital — it is whoever happens to be standing next to the person. This section is about being that person competently.

⚠️ READ THIS BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — what this section is and is not

This is health education, not training and not medical advice. Reading about CPR is to doing CPR what reading about swimming is to swimming. The single most useful action you can take after reading this is to book a certified, in-person, hands-on course — Red Cross / American Heart Association / Resuscitation Council (UK) / your national equivalent — where you compress a real manikin, handle a real (training) AED, and practice an EpiPen trainer. Skills decay; refresh every ~2 years.

Three rules that override everything below: 1. CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES FIRST (or simultaneously). 911 (US/Canada), 112 (EU & most of the world, works from any mobile even with no SIM/signal), 999 (UK), 000 (Australia). Put the phone on speaker — modern dispatchers talk you through CPR, choking, childbirth, naloxone, bleeding control in real time. The dispatcher is part of your team, not a delay. 2. Scene safety first — you are no use as a second casualty. Traffic, fire, electricity, gas, water, violence, fumes. A drowning rescuer who drowns and a bystander electrocuted on the same downed wire are the classic textbook deaths. Look before you leap. 3. Doing something competent beats doing nothing, and doing nothing is the common failure. The dominant problem in cardiac arrest, anaphylaxis, severe bleeding, and opioid overdose is bystander paralysis, not bystander error. The legal cover for this in most jurisdictions is the Good Samaritan framework: an ordinary person acting in good faith, within their training, without gross negligence, is broadly protected. Fear of lawsuits is a poor reason to let someone die.

Cross-references (read alongside): heart attack mechanism, atherosclerosis, and the long-game prevention live in reports/sections/22-disease-cardiometabolic-renal.md §1.1; stroke (the “time is brain” reperfusion revolution, thrombolysis/thrombectomy, FAST/BE-FAST) is owned by reports/sections/24-disease-neuro-rheum.md §3; seizures/epilepsy by 24 §4; sepsis as a disease process and anaphylaxis immunology connect to 15-immune-system.md; heat stroke / hypothermia / cold-water thermal physiology cross-links to 02-domains/H-thermal.md and H-claims.json; drowning & the breath-hold/shallow-water-blackout rule to 02-domains/G-breath.md; opioid pharmacology to 10-medical-pharmacology.md; advance directives / end-of-life to 19-life-stages.md.

1. The mental model — the chain only works if the first link does

Acute medicine has a small number of organizing ideas. Internalize these and most of the specifics follow.

  • The body has a few non-negotiable supply lines — a patent airway, breathing to oxygenate the blood, and circulation to deliver it (the classic A-B-C). Modern lay rescue for collapse reorders this to C-A-B (circulation first) because the commonest reversible adult catastrophe is a heart that has stopped pumping while the blood is still full of oxygen — so chest compressions, not rescue breaths, are the first move. Add D (disability/neuro — stroke, seizure, head injury) and E (exposure/ environment — heat, cold, poison).
  • Hypoxia time is short. The brain begins to suffer irreversible injury after roughly 4–6 minutes without oxygenated blood flow. Professional help, in most of the world, takes longer than that to arrive. That gap — the first 5–10 minutes — is the whole reason laypeople matter. You are not a substitute for the ambulance; you are the bridge that keeps the patient survivable until it arrives.
  • “Recognize → Act” beats “diagnose → treat.” You are not being asked to make a diagnosis. You are being asked to recognize a small set of patterns (“this looks like a stroke,” “this looks like anaphylaxis”) and trigger a small set of actions. Precision is the hospital’s job; speed and pattern-recognition are yours.

1.1 The master “Recognize → Act” table

This is the spine of the section. Each row is expanded later. Print it; put it on a fridge. None of this replaces calling emergency services — every row assumes you have called or are calling.

Emergency Recognize it by (the fast pattern) ACT — the first, highest-leverage move Do NOT
Cardiac arrest Unresponsive and not breathing normally (or only gasping/“agonal” breaths) Call 911 → start hands-only CPR (push hard & fast, center of chest, ~100–120/min) → send for an AED, use it ASAP Don’t check for a pulse if untrained; don’t wait to “be sure”; don’t stop for rescue breaths if untrained
Heart attack (MI) Chest pressure/pain (may radiate to arm/jaw/back), often + sweating, nausea, shortness of breath; atypical in women/elderly/diabetics (fatigue, indigestion, breathlessness) Call 911. Have them sit/rest. Give aspirin 162–325 mg chewed if available, conscious, not allergic, no active bleeding Don’t drive yourself; don’t “wait to see if it passes”; don’t take someone else’s nitroglycerin
Stroke (cross-ref 24 §3) BE-FAST: Balance loss, Eyes (vision), Face droop, Arm drift, Speech slurred → Time Call 911 immediately. Note the exact time symptoms began (decides eligibility for clot-busting/thrombectomy) Don’t give aspirin (could be a bleed); don’t give food/water (swallow may be impaired); don’t “lie down and nap it off”
Anaphylaxis Rapid onset after a trigger: hives + swelling of lips/tongue/throat, wheeze/throat tightness, vomiting, faintness/collapse Epinephrine (EpiPen) into the outer thigh — IMMEDIATELY and FIRST. Call 911. Lie flat, legs up. Repeat epi in 5–15 min if no better Do NOT rely on antihistamines/inhalers as the treatment; don’t stand the person up; don’t delay epi “to see”
Severe bleeding Spurting/pooling blood, soaked clothing, blood that won’t stop Firm direct pressure on the wound, hard, without letting up. If life-threatening limb bleed, apply a tourniquet high & tight Don’t peek/release to “check”; don’t waste time hunting for pressure points; don’t apply a tourniquet loosely
Choking (adult/child) Can’t speak/cough/breathe, clutching throat, silent + panicked 5 back blows between shoulder blades → 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich); alternate. If they collapse → CPR Don’t do blind finger sweeps; don’t do abdominal thrusts on infants/pregnant/obese (use chest thrusts)
Opioid overdose Unresponsive, slow/absent breathing, pinpoint pupils, blue lips/fingertips Naloxone (Narcan) into nostril; call 911; rescue breaths/CPR as needed; repeat naloxone in 2–3 min Don’t assume one dose is enough; don’t leave them alone; don’t delay calling for fear of police (Good Samaritan laws)
Sepsis Infection plus confusion/“acting wrong,” very fast breathing, fast heart, fever or abnormally low temp, mottled skin, not passing urine Call 911 / go to ER. Say the word “sepsis.” Time-to-antibiotics drives survival. Don’t “ride it out at home”; don’t assume normal temp rules it out
Seizure Sudden collapse + rhythmic jerking, eyes open/blank, then confusion Protect head, clear hazards, time it, roll into recovery position once jerking stops. Call 911 if >5 min, first-ever, repeated, injury, pregnancy, or water Do NOT put anything in the mouth; do NOT restrain/hold them down
Severe burn Large, deep, blistering, or on face/hands/genitals/airway Cool with cool (not ice-cold) running water 20 minutes; remove jewelry; cover loosely with clean non-stick material; call for help No butter/oil/toothpaste/ice; don’t burst blisters; don’t peel stuck clothing
Heat stroke (cross-ref H) Hot skin, confusion/collapse, temp ≳40 °C, possibly stopped sweating Call 911. Cool aggressively NOW — cold-water immersion if possible, else ice packs to neck/armpits/groin + wet + fan Don’t wait for the ambulance to start cooling; don’t give fever meds (won’t work)
Hypothermia Shivering → confusion/slurring → shivering stops (ominous), drowsiness Gentle handling, get dry, insulate (incl. head & ground), warm core, warm sweet drinks if fully alert Don’t rub limbs; don’t give alcohol; don’t apply direct scalding heat; handle gently (rough handling can trigger fatal arrhythmia)
Drowning (cross-ref G) Found in/under water, unresponsive; quiet (real drowning is silent, not splashy) Get them out safely (don’t become a victim), check breathing; if absent give rescue breaths then CPR — drowning is a hypoxic arrest, so breaths matter here Don’t attempt deep-water rescue untrained; don’t waste time trying to “drain water from the lungs”

2. Cardiac arrest & the Chain of Survival — the single biggest lever a bystander holds

Cardiac arrest is not a heart attack. A heart attack (myocardial infarction, 22 §1.1) is a plumbing problem — a blocked coronary artery starving heart muscle; the person is usually awake and talking. A cardiac arrest is an electrical problem — the heart’s pumping stops, the person collapses, is unresponsive, and isn’t breathing normally. A heart attack can cause an arrest. The acute action is completely different: heart attack → aspirin + 911 + rest; arrest → CPR + AED now.

Survival from out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) is the canonical “the system is the patient” story. The Chain of Survival (an AHA/ILCOR framework) is only as strong as its first links, and those first links are laypeople:

  1. Early recognition & call for help (you)
  2. Early CPR (you)
  3. Early defibrillation (you + an AED)
  4. Advanced care by EMS
  5. Post-arrest hospital care & recovery

2.1 Hands-only CPR — the evidence it works, and that it’s easier

For an adult who collapses suddenly, compression-only (“hands-only”) CPR by a bystander is recommended as the default — and the evidence is unusually clean:

  • The SOS-KANTO observational study (Lancet 2007) and subsequent trials found compression-only bystander CPR was at least as good as conventional CPR-with-breaths for adult witnessed arrest — and far more people are willing to do it (no mouth-to-mouth barrier). cohort/rct-supported.
  • Bystander CPR roughly doubles to triples survival. A nationwide Swedish study (Hasselqvist-Ax et al., NEJM 2015, 10.1056/NEJMoa1405796) of ~30,000 arrests found 30-day survival of 10.5% with bystander CPR vs 4.0% without — and that early CPR was associated with survival independent of all later links. The intervention with the largest population effect is the one any untrained person can deliver.

How (adult, untrained or rusty — the version worth memorizing): > Push hard, push fast, in the center of the chest. ~100–120 compressions per minute, ~2 inches (5–6 cm) > deep, let the chest fully recoil between each. Don’t stop except to use an AED. Hum Stayin’ Alive or > Baby Shark — both are ~100–110 bpm. Switch with another rescuer every ~2 minutes (it’s exhausting; poor > compressions are the silent failure mode).

For children, infants, drowning, opioid overdose, and any asphyxial cause, oxygen has run down, so rescue breaths add real value — if trained, use 30 compressions : 2 breaths. If not trained, hands-only is still vastly better than nothing. This is a course-skill; book the course.

2.2 AEDs — early defibrillation is the other half of the lever

Most survivable sudden adult arrests start as ventricular fibrillation — a quivering, non-pumping heart. The only thing that fixes VF is an electric shock (defibrillation), and every minute without it drops survival by roughly 7–10%. An Automated External Defibrillator (AED) is built for panicked laypeople: turn it on, it talks you through it, sticks pads where the picture shows, and it will not shock unless it detects a shockable rhythm — you cannot accidentally hurt someone with it.

  • The PAD Trial (Hallstrom et al., NEJM 2004, 10.1056/NEJMoa040566) showed that training community volunteers to use public-access AEDs roughly doubled survivors of OHCA versus CPR alone.
  • Practical rules: send someone to get the AED while you start compressions (don’t stop CPR to go look); map the AEDs near where you live/work (many countries have apps/registries); pads go upper-right chest and lower-left side; resume compressions immediately after a shock. Wet chest → wipe dry; lots of hair → the kit usually has a razor; medication patch → remove it.

2.3 The honest survival statistics

Be clear-eyed: OHCA survival to hospital discharge is only about 8–12% overall, and even with everything done right it is not the TV-CPR ~70%. Why say so? Because (a) it makes the few high-leverage links — bystander CPR + early AED, which can lift witnessed shockable arrest survival above 30–40% — worth fighting for, and (b) it sets honest expectations: bystanders who do excellent CPR on someone who still dies did not fail. They gave the only chance there was. The failure is the arrest no one touched.

3. The time-critical recognitions

3.1 Heart attack — including the atypical and female presentations

The “Hollywood heart attack” (clutching the chest, dropping) is real but partial. The honest picture (cross-ref 22 §1.1):

  • Classic: central chest pressure / tightness / squeezing / heaviness (often described as not sharp), lasting more than a few minutes or coming and going, often radiating to the left arm, both arms, jaw, neck, or back, with cold sweat, nausea, shortness of breath, a sense of doom.
  • Atypical — and dangerously easy to dismiss (more common in women, the elderly, and people with diabetes, whose neuropathy blunts pain): unusual fatigue, breathlessness, indigestion/“heartburn,” jaw or back pain, lightheadedness, nausea — sometimes with little or no chest pain at all. Women are more likely to present this way and, partly because of it, are more likely to be under-triaged and to delay. When in doubt, treat it as cardiac.
  • Act: call 911 (an ambulance can treat an arrest en route — never drive yourself or be driven), rest, and chew (don’t swallow whole) 162–325 mg of aspirin if available, conscious, not allergic, and not actively bleeding — chewing speeds antiplatelet action. Don’t take a stranger’s nitroglycerin.

3.2 Stroke — “time is brain” (owned by 24 §3)

A large-vessel stroke destroys on the order of ~1.9 million neurons per minute (24 §3). Recognition is BE-FAST:

  • Balance — sudden loss of balance/coordination
  • Eyes — sudden vision loss or double vision
  • Face — ask them to smile; does one side droop?
  • Arm — ask them to raise both arms; does one drift down?
  • Speech — slurred, garbled, or unable to find words?
  • Time — note the exact time symptoms started and call 911 now. That timestamp decides eligibility for clot-busting drugs (thrombolysis, ~4.5 h window) and thrombectomy (up to ~24 h in selected patients).

Do not give aspirin for a suspected stroke — until a CT scan rules out a bleed, aspirin could be catastrophic. Do not give food or drink (the swallow may be unsafe). Get them to a stroke-capable hospital by ambulance — the crew pre-alerts the stroke team.

3.3 Anaphylaxis — epinephrine FIRST, and the honest truth about antihistamines

Anaphylaxis is a rapid, multi-system, potentially fatal allergic reaction (food, sting, drug, latex). It typically begins minutes to ~2 hours after exposure with some combination of: hives/flushing/itch, swelling of lips/tongue/throat, throat tightness or hoarse voice, wheeze or trouble breathing, vomiting/ crampy abdominal pain, a sudden drop in blood pressure (faintness, collapse), and a feeling of impending doom. Airway swelling and circulatory collapse are what kill.

The one thing to know: epinephrine is the first-line, life-saving treatment, and the commonest fatal error is delay. (Pumphrey’s classic case series of fatal anaphylaxis found a median time to respiratory/cardiac arrest of minutes, with delayed epinephrine a recurring theme.) The 2020 Joint Task Force practice parameter (10.1016/j.jaci.2020.01.017) and the 2024 international consensus (10.1016/j.jaci.2025.01.021) are unambiguous: epinephrine, intramuscular, into the outer mid-thigh, given immediately. It is extraordinarily safe in this setting; there is no absolute contraindication when anaphylaxis is suspected.

The honest debunk: Antihistamines (Benadryl) and asthma inhalers are NOT treatments for anaphylaxis. Antihistamines treat itch and hives — skin symptoms — and act too slowly to touch airway swelling or shock. Relying on them while the airway closes is a documented path to death. Give epinephrine first; an antihistamine, if any, is a distant afterthought, never a substitute.

Act: EpiPen to the outer thigh (through clothing is fine) → call 911 → lie the person flat with legs raised (sudden standing/sitting up can cause fatal “empty-heart” collapse) → repeat epinephrine in 5–15 minutes if no improvement → everyone who gets epinephrine still needs the ER, because a biphasic reaction can recur hours later. If they carry two auto-injectors, that’s why.

3.4 Sepsis — the subtle one

Sepsis is the body’s dysregulated, life-threatening response to an infection — the immune reaction, not the microbe, becomes the threat (cross-ref 15, 26). It’s a leading cause of death worldwide and it kills partly because it is easy to miss: it can masquerade as “a bad flu” until organs start failing. The signal is an infection PLUS systemic derangement. Lay-recognizable red flags (the UK “Sepsis Six” / “SEPSIS” public messaging):

  • Slurred speech or confusion / “just not acting right”
  • Extreme shivering, fever, or abnormally low temperature (a normal or low temp does NOT rule it out)
  • Passing no urine all day
  • Severe breathlessness / very fast breathing
  • “I feel I might die” — a striking sense of impending doom
  • Skin mottled, blue, or very pale

The Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 guidelines (Evans et al., Crit Care Med 2021, 10.1097/ CCM.0000000000005337) anchor management on early recognition and time-to-antibiotics; the lay job is to escalate fast and say the word “sepsis” to the dispatcher/triage nurse — it changes how quickly they’re seen. Children: add not feeding, repeated vomiting, a non-blanching rash (a rash that doesn’t fade under pressure — the “glass test” — is a meningococcal-sepsis emergency).

3.5 Severe bleeding — the modern update

The doctrine here changed with the wars of the 2000s and the “Stop the Bleed” public campaign. Old caution about tourniquets (“last resort, you’ll lose the limb”) was overcorrected and is now considered wrong for life-threatening extremity bleeding.

  • First and almost always enough: firm, direct, sustained pressure right on the wound — your gloved hand (or a clean cloth, shirt, anything) pressed hard and not lifted to peek. Pack deep wounds with gauze/cloth and keep pressing.
  • If a limb is bleeding so fast it’s life-threatening (spurting, pooling, won’t stop): apply a tourniquet high on the limb (“high and tight,” 2–3 inches above the wound, not over a joint), tighten until the bleeding stops (it will hurt — that’s expected), and note the time. Kragh et al. (Ann Surg 2009, 10.1097/SLA.0b013e31818842ba) showed in combat casualties that tourniquets applied before shock onset dramatically improved survival, with limb loss being rare and usually due to the injury, not the tourniquet. A properly applied tourniquet saves lives; a loose one just hides the bleeding. Do not remove it — that’s the hospital’s call.
  • Get a real Stop the Bleed course; the kit (tourniquet + hemostatic gauze) is cheap and belongs anywhere trauma is plausible (cars, worksites, schools).

3.6 Choking

  • Recognize: sudden inability to speak, cough, or breathe; the universal hands-at-the-throat clutch; silence and panic. A person who can still cough forcefully has a partial obstruction — encourage the cough, don’t intervene. It’s the silent choker who needs you.
  • Act (responsive adult/child): 5 sharp back blows between the shoulder blades (lean them forward), then 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich): fist above the navel, sharp inward-and-upward thrusts. Alternate 5 and 5 until the object clears or they collapse.
  • If they go unconscious: lower them, start CPR, and check the mouth for a visible object before breaths (remove only what you can see — no blind finger sweeps, which push it deeper).
  • Special cases: infants — 5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts (never abdominal thrusts). Pregnant or very obese adults — chest thrusts instead of abdominal. Yourself, alone — abdominal thrusts against a chair back or counter edge.

3.7 Opioid overdose — the practical epidemic angle

The opioid epidemic made naloxone (Narcan) the single most important first-aid drug of this era for laypeople. Overdose looks like: unresponsive, breathing slow/shallow/absent, pinpoint pupils, blue/grey lips and fingertips, gurgling/snoring. Death comes from respiratory depression — they stop breathing.

  • Naloxone is an opioid antagonist that reverses it within minutes. It’s now widely available over the counter as a nasal spray, is safe to give even if you’re wrong (it does nothing to a non-opioid cause), and is the textbook case for “carry it, the way you’d carry an EpiPen if you knew someone at risk.”
  • Walley et al. (BMJ 2013, 10.1136/bmj.f174) showed that community Overdose Education & Naloxone Distribution (OEND) — putting naloxone in the hands of laypeople — was associated with significantly lower opioid-overdose death rates at the population level. Supply-side reversal works.
  • Act: spray naloxone into one nostril → call 911 → support breathing (rescue breaths / CPR as needed) → repeat naloxone every 2–3 minutes if no response (today’s fentanyl-dominant supply often needs multiple doses) → stay with them — naloxone wears off in 30–90 min and the opioid can outlast it, so they can re-overdose. Good Samaritan overdose laws in most US states protect callers from drug- possession charges — call anyway.

4. First aid: evidence-based vs. myth

A surprising amount of “common knowledge” first aid is wrong, useless, or harmful. The grading principle of this manual (06-evidence/SCHEMA.md) applies: a confident folk remedy is anecdotal-tier until a real source says otherwise.

4.1 Burns

  • Do: cool with cool (not ice-cold) running water for ~20 minutes, ideally within the first 3 hours. This is genuinely evidence-based — adequate cool-water first aid reduces burn depth, the need for grafting, and scarring (supported by clinical/cohort burn-registry data; e.g. cooling-duration analyses). Remove rings/watches/tight items before swelling starts. Cover loosely with cling film or a clean non-fluffy cloth. Treat pain with normal painkillers.
  • DON’T — the classic harmful myths:
    • No butter, oil, toothpaste, egg, or “natural” pastes. They trap heat, seed infection, and have to be painfully scrubbed off later. Butter on a burn is a genuinely bad idea, full stop.
    • No ice or ice water. Too cold causes vasoconstriction and deepens the injury (a cold-burn on top of a heat-burn). Cool, not freezing.
    • Don’t burst blisters (the roof is a sterile dressing). Don’t peel away clothing stuck to the burn.
  • Go to the ER for burns that are: large (> a palm-size area), deep/white/charred/painless (full-thickness kills the nerves), on the face, hands, feet, genitals, or over a joint, circumferential, electrical or chemical, or any airway/inhalation burn (singed nostril hair, soot, hoarse voice — the airway can swell shut).

4.2 Nosebleeds — the head-tilt myth

Debunk: Do NOT tilt the head back. That just sends blood down the throat to be swallowed (nausea, vomiting, and you can’t see if it’s stopping). Lean forward, pinch the soft part of the nose (not the bony bridge) firmly for 10–15 uninterrupted minutes — no peeking. Sit upright. Seek care if it won’t stop after ~20–30 minutes, follows a head injury, or the person is on blood thinners.

4.3 Sprains, strains & soft-tissue injury — RICE is retired

The old RICE (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation) mnemonic has been superseded (cross-ref the rehab section 21-pain-injury-rehab.md). The current sports-medicine framework is PEACE & LOVE (Dubois & Esculier, Br J Sports Med 2020, 10.1136/bjsports-2019-101253): brief Protection, Elevation, avoid anti-inflammatory over-use, Compression, Education — then, crucially, Load, Optimism, Vascularisation (movement), Exercise. The headline shift: prolonged rest and aggressive icing are not the goal — early, graded, optimistic loading is. (Acute first aid for the first day still uses relative rest, support, and ice for pain control — just don’t camp there.) Always rule out a fracture: deformity, can’t bear weight/use it, point tenderness over bone, numbness → image it.

4.4 Fractures & “is it broken?”

You usually can’t be sure without an X-ray, so treat a suspected fracture as a fracture. Immobilize it in the position found (don’t try to straighten it unless the limb is pulseless/blue and you’re trained), support above and below the injury, control any bleeding, and arrange transport. Open fractures (bone through skin) and suspected spine/neck injuries (don’t move them unless they’re in immediate danger — fire, water; keep the head/neck aligned) are emergencies. Suspect spine injury after falls from height, diving, high-speed crashes, or any unconscious trauma patient.

4.5 Head injury — the red flags

Most bumps to the head are minor. Watch for the bleed-inside signals in the hours after, and go to the ER for any of: loss of consciousness (even briefly), repeated vomiting, worsening or “worst-ever” headache, confusion/drowsiness/hard to wake, seizure, unequal pupils, weakness/numbness, clear fluid or blood from nose/ears, a dangerous mechanism (high-speed, fall >~1 m / 5 stairs), or anyone on blood thinners (bleeds can be slow and large). For sport, the rule is “if in doubt, sit them out” — a second impact before recovery can be catastrophic.

4.6 Seizures — what NOT to do is the whole lesson

The two cardinal don’ts: Do NOT put anything in the mouth (the “swallow their tongue” idea is a myth — you’ll break teeth, get bitten, or block the airway) and do NOT hold them down / restrain them. - Do: note the start time, ease them to the floor, clear hard/sharp objects away, cushion the head, loosen anything tight at the neck, and once the jerking stops, roll them into the recovery position to protect the airway while they come round (they’ll be confused — “postictal” — for a while; stay, reassure). - Call 911 if: it lasts >5 minutes or repeats without recovery (status epilepticus — a true emergency), it’s a first-ever seizure, there’s injury, it happens in water, the person is pregnant or diabetic, or they don’t come round.

4.7 The recovery position

For anyone unconscious but breathing normally (not in cardiac arrest), roll them onto their side so the tongue falls forward and any vomit drains out rather than into the lungs. It is the default holding position while you wait for help, and it converts “unconscious on their back” (airway at risk) into “unconscious and protected.” (If you suspect a spine injury and they’re breathing, this is a judgment call — maintaining the airway wins over a theoretical spine concern if they’re vomiting.)

4.8 Quick-hit myth debunks

Myth Reality
Suck the venom out of a snakebite / cut and suck Useless and harmful. Keep the limb still and below heart level, remove tight items, get to antivenom. No tourniquet, no ice, no incision, no suction.
Pee on a jellyfish sting Not supported and can worsen some stings. Rinse with vinegar (for many species) or hot water (~45 °C) immersion; remove tentacles without bare hands; seek care for box-jelly/systemic symptoms.
Tilt head back for a nosebleed Lean forward, pinch the soft nose 10–15 min (see §4.2).
Butter / ice on a burn Cool running water 20 min; nothing greasy, nothing frozen (§4.1).
Rub a frostbitten or hypothermic limb to warm it Don’t — friction damages tissue and can trigger arrhythmia. Rewarm gently and steadily; no snow-rubbing.
Slap a choking person’s back while they’re still coughing If they can cough/speak, let them cough. Intervene only when the cough fails (§3.6).
A swallowed tongue in seizures Anatomically impossible. Nothing in the mouth (§4.6).
You should drain water from a drowning victim’s lungs No — start rescue breaths and CPR; “draining” wastes time and risks aspiration of stomach contents (§6.3).
Tourniquets always cost the limb Modern evidence: properly applied, they save lives and limb loss is rare (§3.5).
Hyperventilate / breath-hold to swim further underwater Dangerous — causes shallow-water blackout and silent drowning (cross-ref G-breath.md, §6.3).

5. Triage: ER vs. urgent care vs. wait — the honest version

People die from under-triage (waiting out a stroke) and waste fortunes / clog the system from over-triage (an ER visit for a cold). The honest middle:

Call 911 / go to the ER immediately (the red flags — never “wait and see”): - Chest pain/pressure, especially with sweating, nausea, breathlessness, or radiating pain - Any BE-FAST stroke sign — face droop, arm drift, speech trouble, sudden vision/balance loss - Trouble breathing — can’t speak full sentences, blue lips, gasping, severe wheeze - Anaphylaxis — throat/tongue swelling, widespread hives + breathing/faintness - “Worst headache of my life” / thunderclap headache (possible brain bleed) - Severe uncontrolled bleeding, or major trauma (high-speed, fall from height) - Sudden severe abdominal pain, coughing/vomiting blood, black tarry stools - Unresponsiveness, a first or prolonged seizure, sudden confusion - Signs of sepsis (§3.4), stiff neck + fever + rash (meningitis), suicidal intent (cross-ref 20) - A fever in a baby <3 months, or a child who is floppy, blue, hard to wake, or has a non-blanching rash
